question: What did Apollo astronauts actually do on the lunar surface, and what did they bring back?

sub_questions: What activities did Apollo astronauts perform during lunar surface EVAs (walks) — e.g., sampling, deploying experiments, traversing with a rover?
What tools, instruments and hardware did they carry onto and use on the surface?
What physical items did they bring back to Earth (rocks, regolith, film, experiment hardware/data)?
How were the surface activities organized in sequence during an EVA and across EVAs (chronology of tasks and stowage)?
phrasings: What did Apollo astronauts actually do on the lunar surface, and what did they bring back?
Astronauts performed extravehicular activities on the lunar surface, collecting samples and deploying experiments.
Astronauts collected rock and soil samples and stowed them in sample bags and containment boxes for return to Earth.
The crew deployed the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package and other scientific instruments on the Moon.
Astronauts used the Lunar Roving Vehicle to extend their exploration range across the plain.
Astronauts loaded tools, film magazines and sample containers into the rover and lunar module for return.
Crews documented their work with photography and returned film, data and lunar samples to Earth.
visual_phrasings: Close-up of astronauts' boots in lunar regolith, using scoops and tongs to pick up rocks and soil.
Astronauts placing sealed sample bags and sample boxes into the lunar module cargo area or into the rover's stowage.

plan.rationale: I broke the question into EVA tasks, surface tools/instruments, returned materials, and the sequence of activities so searches match NASA narration about what was done, what was used, and what was brought back.

answer.answer: Taken together, the clips show astronauts descending a lander ladder and walking on the bright, dusty lunar surface (bootprints and descent shown) while wearing life‑support backpacks and carrying cameras [6][8][9].  They used long‑handled sampling tools and core samplers while crouching or standing to collect rocks and regolith (lunar soil) [3][4].  Commentary and footage emphasize choosing and collecting rock samples for later study, indicating the surface work produced curated rock and soil samples for scientific analysis [9][3].  Other archival material in the set is not surface EVA footage but hardware assembly and scientific diagrams about lunar regolith and hydrogen content, so the archive mixes surface activities with ground and animated material [1][2].

chronology.claim: The archive for this period includes spacecraft hardware assembly and test footage rather than only lunar surface EVA footage.

answer.caveats: The clips show sampling and sample‑selection activity but do not by themselves document how many samples were returned, where they were stored, or confirm that particular samples were returned to Earth; those inferences are not established by the provided clips [3][9].  Also, some item dates in the evidence are derived from era_axis: video or published metadata rather than independent confirmation of the event dates, so the dating indicated in the clips may not be certain [1][2].

evidence.query: Crew members assembling and deploying surface experiments and the unfolded panels of an experiment package.
evidence.text: A montage shows spacecraft hardware and assembly/testing scenes rather than planetary surface footage. In the upper left, a cleanroom worker in a white protective suit stands in a red cherry-picker lift beside a large folded, gold-and-black space instrument or telescope component. Other panels show a cylindrical spacecraft bus wrapped in gold thermal insulation being handled by technicians in a cleanroom, close-ups of dark solar-panel surfaces and structural hardware, and an older archival shot of technicians around a small spacecraft during assembly. The lower panels show an interior view looking through a window at a circular spacecraft structure or docking target, paired with a separate shot of a small satellite with two rectangular solar arrays floating against black space. The overall scene suggests satellite/telescope integration, deployment, and orbital operations around Earth, with no planetary surface visible.
evidence.title: Goddard at 60

evidence.query: Close-up of astronauts' boots in lunar regolith, using scoops and tongs to pick up rocks and soil.
evidence.text: The scene shows a blue-toned animated diagram of lunar regolith texture, with clusters of small red and pale-blue spheres representing particles or atoms dispersed within the soil. A highlighted single pale sphere appears at left, and the display switches between two labeled states: “Low Hydrogen Soil” and “High Hydrogen Soil.” No spacecraft, landscape, or physical instrument is shown; this is an explanatory animation about how hydrogen content in lunar soil affects neutron measurements.
evidence.title: Water on the Moon

evidence.query: Close-up of astronauts' boots in lunar regolith, using scoops and tongs to pick up rocks and soil.
evidence.text: Archival, low-resolution black-and-white footage showing two suited astronauts working on a flat, gray lunar surface. The foreground shows two figures in bulky extravehicular suits with rectangular life‑support backpacks standing close together. One astronaut is holding a long sampling tool or core‑sampler (a pole/auger) upright while the other appears to be manipulating or inserting the tool into the regolith. The ground is featureless and powdery with visible footprints and shallow disturbed areas around the tool. The sky is black and featureless behind them; the horizon is low in the frame. Subsequent frames in the sequence cut to space imagery showing a small, free‑flying scientific object or satellite with long, thin booms or antennae extending from a central body against a dark background. The space shots are also low resolution and monochrome, showing the deployed object moving away from a darker spacecraft silhouette.
evidence.title: 1971 Aeronautics and Space Highlights

evidence.query: Crew members assembling and deploying surface experiments and the unfolded panels of an experiment package.
evidence.text: Interior hangar and laboratory footage showing aerospace test hardware and an interview. Multiple close-up shots of aircraft fuselage sections and test rigs: stripped jet noses and cockpit areas with exposed wiring and avionics racks, freestanding instrument cabinets with red wiring panels, circular test fixtures, and yellow lifting straps attached to components. Overhead gantry cranes and cable runs are visible. A wide shot shows a large clean hangar floor with a circular test stand, rows of equipment boxes, cable troughs, and an American flag on the far wall; a NASA logo appears on a doorway or panel in the background. The segment ends with a medium close-up of a man in a white shirt and patterned tie speaking to camera, with technicians and large cylindrical/hypothetical test articles blurred behind him. Burned-in on-screen text reads 'NAVY NASA NASA.' No mission name or specific date is shown.
evidence.title: AFRC 75th Anniversary Series Episode 10- Flight Loads
